findings.message: DeleteNoteCommand.execute() is a stub that does not remove any note from the model. It only returns a success message ('Delete note request received for date: %1$s') without calling any model operation. The note is never actually deleted. This makes the advertised `note d-/DATE` feature entirely non-functional.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: DeleteNoteCommand.execute() at lines 35-38 only calls requireNonNull and returns a CommandResult with a placeholder message. It never calls model.removeNote() or any equivalent. The note deletion feature is non-functional.
findings.severity_justification: The advertised `note d-/DATE` command silently appears to succeed but does nothing, leaving notes permanently in the address book with no way to remove them.
findings.category_justification: The command's execute method fails to perform the operation it is supposed to — it is a logic stub masquerading as a working feature.

findings.message: The Model interface has no removeNote() method, even though AddressBook.removeNote() exists. There is no path from any command through Model to AddressBook for note deletion. Even if DeleteNoteCommand.execute() were fixed, it would have no model API to call.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: Model interface only declares setNote() and getPlannerNoteProperty() — no removeNote(). Even though AddressBook.removeNote() exists (as shown in the diff), there is no Model interface method, no ModelManager override, and therefore no way for DeleteNoteCommand to call note removal even if its execute() were fixed.
findings.severity_justification: The delete-note feature is architecturally incomplete: the entire Model API layer for note deletion is missing, making it impossible to implement DeleteNoteCommand.execute() correctly without further interface changes.
findings.category_justification: The gap is in the Model interface — a missing method in the public API contract — which is an API/architecture concern distinct from the stub implementation bug in DeleteNoteCommand.

findings.message: DeleteNoteCommand does not override isStateMutating(), so it inherits the default return value of false. When note deletion is eventually implemented, delete operations will not participate in undo/redo state capture, making them non-undoable unlike NoteCommand which correctly returns true.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: Command base class defaults isStateMutating() to false. DeleteNoteCommand does not override it. NoteCommand (updated in this PR) correctly overrides it to true. The missing override means delete operations will not be undoable when eventually implemented.
findings.severity_justification: The command is currently non-functional anyway, but the missing isStateMutating() override represents a real gap that would produce a silent undo/redo regression when the delete is eventually implemented, and a developer fixing the execute() stub might not think to add it.
findings.category_justification: Missing override of a behavioral method that controls state-mutation tracking — a logic correctness issue for the command lifecycle.

findings.message: The notes field is initialized as new HashMap<>(), which does not preserve insertion order. AddressBook uses LinkedHashMap specifically to maintain a consistent iteration order for note merging. After a save/reload cycle, the order notes are iterated in updatePlannerNote() will be non-deterministic, causing the merged note display order to differ between sessions when multiple notes apply to the same date (e.g., an 'everyday' note and a specific-date note).
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: JsonSerializableAddressBook uses new HashMap<>() for notes (line 29), while AddressBook uses LinkedHashMap (line 35). On deserialization, setNote() is called in HashMap's non-deterministic iteration order, corrupting the LinkedHashMap's carefully maintained insertion order. updatePlannerNote() iterates in this order when merging, so the merged display will differ between sessions.
findings.severity_justification: The actual data is preserved; only the display order of merged notes may change between sessions. No data is lost, and in practice most users will have at most one or two notes per date. The UX impact is minor.
findings.category_justification: This is an ordering consistency issue introduced by the storage/deserialization path that causes non-deterministic behavior across sessions.

findings.message: execute_deleteNote_success() uses an empty model and an empty expectedModel, so the test trivially passes without exercising deletion. A note added before the command would still be present in the model after execution, but this is never verified. The test provides no coverage of the core delete behavior.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: setUp() creates two empty ModelManager instances. The test never adds a note to model before running the command. assertCommandSuccess only checks message equality and model equality — both models are empty and unchanged, so equality holds trivially. The test provides zero coverage of actual deletion behavior.
findings.severity_justification: The test is weak, but given that the underlying DeleteNoteCommand is already a known stub (Finding 1), this is unsurprising — the test reflects the stub's non-behavior. The severity is low since fixing the real bug (stub execute) would require reworking this test anyway.
findings.category_justification: The finding is specifically about inadequate test coverage — a test that trivially passes without exercising the behavior it purports to test.

findings.message: setNote() only calls updatePlannerNote() when date.isOn(currentPlannedDate) is true. This correctly handles most cases, but does not handle the case where a note was already displayed for the current date via a matching key (e.g., 'everyday') and the user adds a new note for the same date key, overwriting it with a different date type. While the overwrite updates the map, the planner note isn't refreshed unless the new date key's isOn() also returns true for the current view date. In practice this is unlikely but the conditional logic is subtly asymmetric with how the map key is matched.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The described scenario ('overwriting with a different date type') is incoherent - different VisitDate type/value combinations produce different map keys and cannot overwrite each other. The isOn() check in setNote() is semantically correct: it refreshes the planner only when the newly-set note's date actually applies to the currently-viewed date. No concrete failing scenario exists.
findings.severity_justification: Since the claim is factually incorrect, no real bug exists.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges a logic bug in the conditional update path.

findings.message: hashCode() uses simple addition: locations.hashCode() + notes.hashCode(). This produces the same hash for any two AddressBook instances where the component hashCodes are swapped (e.g., locations=3, notes=5 and locations=5, notes=3), increasing collision frequency compared to Objects.hash(locations, notes). While the contract is not violated, this is weaker than the standard approach.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: hashCode() at line 175 uses addition, which is symmetric and produces the same value if component hashes are swapped. The hashCode contract is not violated, but Objects.hash(locations, notes) is the idiomatic, stronger alternative. The finding is factually correct.
findings.severity_justification: This is a sub-optimal but valid hashCode implementation. The contract is intact, and collision-amplification scenarios are academic in this context where AddressBook instances are compared in tests and equality checks, not inserted into high-cardinality hash structures.
findings.category_justification: This is a code quality / best-practice issue with no runtime correctness impact — a style/idiom concern about using the standard Objects.hash() pattern.

findings.message: The VALIDATION_REGEX was changed to (?s)[^\s].* to support embedded newlines in system-generated merged notes. However, NoteContent is also the type used for user-provided input. With this change, a user can now create a NoteContent with embedded newlines if they bypass the CLI (e.g., via direct JSON editing). More concretely, updatePlannerNote() wraps a multi-line system string in a NoteContent object, blurring the boundary between user-facing and internal data. The merged note should use a separate type or plain String in the UI layer rather than reusing NoteContent with relaxed validation.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: VALIDATION_REGEX was changed to (?s)[^\s].* specifically because updatePlannerNote() wraps multi-line system strings in NoteContent. This relaxes validation for user-provided input as well, blurring the boundary between user data and system-generated merged content. The finding's factual claims about dual usage of NoteContent are correct.
findings.severity_justification: No data is lost or corrupted. CLI users can't inject newlines easily, and JSON editing is a non-standard path. The design concern is real but has negligible practical impact.
findings.category_justification: The issue is about type design — user-facing validation type being repurposed for internal system data, causing the validation contract to be loosened for an internal concern.

findings.message: The `setNote` call in the `execute` method does not handle potential errors such as null dates or note content, which could lead to runtime exceptions.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The constructor calls requireNonNull(noteContent) and requireNonNull(date), and both fields are final. Null values at execute() time are structurally impossible. The finding is a generic null-safety warning that doesn't reflect the actual code.
findings.severity_justification: No real risk exists given the constructor guards.
findings.category_justification: The finding claims a potential runtime exception risk.

findings.message: The `PlannerListPanel` initializes the note display only if `plannerNote.getValue()` is non-null; this might result in an incomplete UI update if the value changes unexpectedly later.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The listener handles all future value changes unconditionally (including null). The initial null-guard skips calling showNote(null) at construction time, but since showNote(null) just clears an already-empty container, skipping it is a no-op. There is no scenario where 'later' changes are missed — the listener covers all of them.
findings.severity_justification: No real bug exists.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges an incomplete UI update — a runtime behavior concern.

findings.message: The `setNotes` method in `AddressBook` should validate the map entirely before modifying the internal state to ensure consistency, as partial updates could leave the object in an invalid state.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The setNotes method validates the entire input map via forEach before calling this.notes.clear() and putAll(). If any null entry is found during validation, NPE is thrown before state mutation occurs. The finding's claim about partial updates causing invalid state does not reflect the actual code structure.
findings.severity_justification: The concern is unfounded given the code already validates fully before modifying state.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges a potential state consistency issue.

findings.message: The deserialization logic for notes does not validate the VisitDate keys and NoteContent values before adding them to the AddressBook, potentially allowing invalid data to be loaded.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The deserialization code does validate: VisitDate.of(dateKey) throws IllegalValueException for invalid dates; noteValue is explicitly null-checked; NoteContent.isValidNoteContent() is called before construction. All invalid data paths throw IllegalValueException which propagates through toModelType(). The finding is factually wrong.
findings.severity_justification: No real validation gap exists.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges missing input validation in deserialization.

findings.message: `setNote` directly updates the AddressBook and planner, but lacks transactional safeguards; if an exception occurs, the in-memory AddressBook state could become inconsistent with the planner note.
findings.tp_fp_justification: No realistic exception path exists between addressBook.setNote() and updatePlannerNote(). addressBook.setNote() is a typed LinkedHashMap.put() that can't throw after null checks pass. updatePlannerNote() builds from already-validated NoteContent values. The finding restates a general defensive-programming principle without identifying any concrete failure mode in this code.
findings.severity_justification: No real inconsistency scenario exists in practice.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about potential state inconsistency — a reliability concern.

findings.message: The `updatePlannerNote` method assumes that all notes can be retrieved correctly and concatenated without verification; invalid or corrupted notes might cause unexpected behavior.
findings.tp_fp_justification: NoteContent objects are immutable and validated at construction/deserialization time. The map only contains already-validated entries. The method only calls .toString() and StringBuilder.append(), which cannot throw. There is no realistic path for 'invalid or corrupted notes' to reach this code. The finding is a generic warning with no concrete failure scenario.
findings.severity_justification: No real risk exists given the invariants maintained by NoteContent and the storage layer.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about potential unexpected behavior from bad data — a reliability concern.

findings.message: The `VALIDATION_REGEX` does not handle cases where only whitespace is included after line breaks, potentially allowing invalid notes with only whitespace after newline characters.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The regex intentionally only prevents blank/empty notes by requiring the first character to be non-whitespace. Having whitespace after newlines in a multi-line note is not invalid by design. User input is trimmed before validation; system-generated notes come from already-validated content. The showNote() method also guards against blank content. No concrete invalid-note scenario exists.
findings.severity_justification: No real validation gap with practical impact.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges the validation regex permits invalid input.

findings.message: The `PlannerListPanel` does not handle the possibility of `newValue` being null during plannerNote updates, which could lead to UI inconsistencies.
findings.tp_fp_justification: showNote() explicitly checks 'note == null' at line 68 before any UI operation. When newValue is null, the method clears the note container and returns, which is the correct behavior (clearing the displayed note). The listener correctly delegates null handling to showNote().
findings.severity_justification: No real issue exists; null is fully handled.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges a null-handling gap causing UI inconsistency.

findings.message: In the deserialization process, `null` values in the notes map are not explicitly checked or rejected, leading to potential NullPointerExceptions if accessed later.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Line 74 explicitly checks 'if (noteValue == null)' and throws IllegalValueException with a descriptive message. The finding claims null values are not checked, but the check is present in the code at the exact lines referenced.
findings.severity_justification: No real issue exists; null values are explicitly handled.
findings.category_justification: The finding alleges missing null handling leading to NPE.

findings.message: The `removeNote_existingDate_removesNote` test does not verify that other notes remain unaffected after a specific note is removed, which weakens the test's robustness.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Factually correct: the test only operates on a single note and never verifies isolation (that other notes remain after removal). Adding a second note and asserting it persists post-removal would strengthen the test. The claim is accurate.
findings.severity_justification: The underlying implementation is a simple LinkedHashMap.remove() which cannot affect other entries. The missing assertion addresses a theoretical gap with near-zero real-world risk.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about test coverage completeness — a missing assertion in a unit test.

findings.tp_fp_justification: This is a generic refactoring suggestion ('could be refactored as a NoteManager class') that could be copy-pasted onto any codebase that adds a new concern to an existing class. It names no specific code problem, inconsistency, or violation — just a general SRP preference. There is no concrete issue identified in the actual code.

findings.category_justification: The suggestion is about code organization and separation of concerns.

findings.message: The test name `constructor_nullLocations_success` is misleading because the test also passes `null` for the `notes` argument. Consider renaming it to something like `constructor_nullArguments_success` to accurately reflect what is being tested.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the test at line 68 calls `new JsonSerializableAddressBook(null, null)`, passing null for both arguments, but is named `constructor_nullLocations_success` — omitting that notes is also null. The name is factually inaccurate for what the test exercises.
findings.severity_justification: Misleading test name is a minor maintainability issue with no behavioral impact, but it reduces the clarity of the test suite.
findings.category_justification: The issue is a naming inaccuracy in a test method that reduces code readability and clarity.

findings.message: The new note deserialization path validates date keys, null values, and invalid note content, but the storage tests only cover a successful note round-trip. Please add failure cases similar to the existing invalid/duplicate location tests so corrupted persisted notes report IllegalValueException instead of regressing silently.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `JsonSerializableAddressBook.toModelType()` has three explicit error branches for notes (invalid date key, null note value, invalid note content), but `JsonSerializableAddressBookTest` only tests the success path. Comparable failure tests exist for locations but not notes, creating a real coverage gap.
findings.severity_justification: The error paths do exist and throw correctly; this is missing test coverage rather than a functional bug. Storage corruption would surface at startup anyway, but not having regression tests means future changes could silently break the validation.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about missing test cases for error paths in the storage deserialization layer.

findings.message: This updated note example is still in a section that says notes are only syntax-validated and will be persisted in future milestones. Since notes are now implemented and persisted, the surrounding user-facing description should be updated so users are not told the feature is still deferred.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the description at line 334 still says 'will be persisted in future milestones. Currently, it validates syntax via CLI and confirms receipt.' This PR fully implements note persistence and model integration, making this description factually incorrect and misleading to users. The PR only updated the example, not the surrounding text.
findings.severity_justification: This is user-facing documentation that explicitly tells users the feature is deferred/not yet functional, when it is now fully working. A user reading this would incorrectly believe notes are not actually saved.
findings.category_justification: The issue is stale/misleading user-facing documentation in the UserGuide.

findings.message: The new mutating flag is only asserted directly in NoteCommandTest, but there is no end-to-end undo/redo test exercising a note command through LogicManager even though other mutating commands have that coverage. Please add a test that runs `note`, `undo`, and `redo` and verifies the note map/planner note is restored correctly.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: LogicManagerTest has execute_undoRedoAddressBookChange_success (using add) and execute_undoRedoShortcutChange_success (using shortcut set), but no equivalent test for the note command. NoteCommandTest only asserts isStateMutating() is true, not the full undo/redo cycle. The note map restoration through resetData/setNotes is a new path not covered by existing tests.
findings.severity_justification: The undo/redo mechanism is generic and well-tested for other commands. The note-specific state restoration follows the same pattern, so the risk of regression is low. This is a test coverage gap rather than a likely bug.
findings.category_justification: The finding identifies a missing integration test for the undo/redo flow of the new note command.

findings.message: The resetData path now copies global notes, but the AddressBook tests only exercise resetData with location-only data. Please add a test with notes in the source ReadOnlyAddressBook so regressions where notes are dropped during reset/copy are caught.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the three resetData tests use getTypicalAddressBook() (no notes) or AddressBookStub (returns emptyMap for getNoteMap()). No test passes a ReadOnlyAddressBook with notes to resetData, so the new setNotes call is not covered. A regression that dropped notes during reset/copy would go undetected.
findings.severity_justification: The implementation looks correct (setNotes is called), so this is a coverage gap rather than a bug. Risk of silent regression is real but low since the logic is simple.
findings.category_justification: The finding identifies a missing test case for the updated resetData code path.

findings.message: If setNotes is called with this AddressBook's own getNoteMap() (for example via resetData(this)), this clears the backing map before putAll reads from it, so all notes are lost. Copy the incoming entries to a temporary map before clearing the internal map.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The self-aliasing issue is real: `getNoteMap()` returns a live view (`Collections.unmodifiableMap(notes)`), so `this.notes.clear()` before `putAll` would silently lose all notes if called with the same object's map. While no current call site triggers this, the latent fragility is a genuine correctness concern and the analogous location path handles self-aliasing safely via ObservableList.setAll().
findings.severity_justification: No current code path triggers this — resetData is always called with a separate object. The risk is confined to future misuse of the API or tests that call resetData(this), not any live user-facing flow.
findings.category_justification: The finding identifies a latent data-loss bug in the setNotes method when called with a self-referential view map.
